q: Before the Indian Ocean crossing a crew member looks at the plotter and asks why the great-circle track, which curves far south of the straight line on the chart, is the shorter one. What do you tell them?
a: Its plane passes through the Earth's centre — the shortest way on a sphere
o: It keeps one course, so no miles are lost in turns
The plotter allows for the east-going current in the forties
It follows the line along which magnetic variation stays the same
why: A great circle is cut by a plane through the Earth's centre; its shorter arc is the shortest route between two points on the globe.
ref: Great circle sailing — the shortest route

lines: GC track bows south to about 44½°S

q: You draw a straight line from Halifax to Falmouth on this gnomonic chart. What does the line show?
a: The great-circle track between the two ports
o: The rhumb line — one course all the way
The track along the parallel of mean latitude
The route the pilot chart recommends for June
why: On a gnomonic chart every great circle is a straight line; a rhumb line on it is curved.
ref: Great circle sailing — the gnomonic chart

q: With the great circle drawn on the gnomonic chart, a crew member picks up the protractor and dividers to take the course and the distance off it. What do you tell them?
a: Neither is true on this chart: transfer the points or compute
o: Fine — courses and distances are both true on it
The course is true; measure the distance on the edge
The distance is true; take the course from the rose
why: A gnomonic chart shows great circles as straight lines but distorts angles and distances; use it only to pick the points.
ref: Great circle sailing — the gnomonic chart

q: Which of the three tracks on this Mercator chart is the great circle from Cape Town to Fremantle?
a: C — it bows south, towards the pole
o: A — it bows north, towards the equator
B — the straight line between the ports
A or C — it depends on the way you sail
why: On a Mercator chart a great circle bows towards the nearer pole — south in the southern hemisphere; the straight line B is the rhumb line.
ref: Great circle sailing — on the Mercator chart

fig.note: Mercator chart, south Indian Ocean (north up)

q: You have drawn the great circle from Halifax to Falmouth on the gnomonic chart. How do you put it on the Mercator chart you navigate by?
a: Read its latitude on every 10° meridian and plot those points
o: Measure the initial course and lay it off from Halifax
Copy the straight line across at the same angle
Lay off the distance along the rhumb line
why: Take the latitude where the GC crosses each meridian 5° or 10° apart, plot the points on the Mercator chart and join them with short rhumb lines.

q: You rule this straight line from Mindelo to Barbados on the Mercator chart and set the autopilot to the one course it gives. What track are you sailing?
a: A rhumb line, crossing every meridian at the same angle
o: A great circle, the shortest track
A composite track along a limiting latitude
A parallel sailing along one latitude
why: A straight line on a Mercator chart is a rhumb line: one course, the same angle with every meridian — but not the shortest track.

q: Heading south through the Atlantic you have this leg in the plotter. Your watch leader suggests switching it to GC to save miles. How much does it save?
a: Nothing — a meridian is itself a great circle
o: About 12 M — about 1 % of the leg
About 60 M — about 5 % of the leg
About 120 M — about 10 % of the leg
why: Meridians and the equator are great circles and rhumb lines at once: on a due north–south leg GC and RL are the same track.

q: You compare four ocean passages. On which does the great circle save the most miles over the rhumb line?
why: The saving grows with latitude and east–west distance: about 214 M Cape Town–Fremantle, 32 M St John's–Falmouth, 10 M ARC, 0 M north–south.

q: From this waypoint you could run due east along the parallel to Falmouth or take the great circle. How much shorter is the great circle?
why: Parallel: 1,796′ of DLo × cos 50.15° = 1,151 M; the GC is 1,143 M. Even a due-east leg is not the shortest away from the equator.

q: On the Puddle Jump you wonder whether to switch the plotter to GC. How much shorter is the great circle?
why: GC 2,996 M against RL 2,997 M: so close to the equator the two tracks almost coincide.

q: You are about to leave St John's for Falmouth with the plotter set as shown. How many miles would the great circle save?
why: GC by cos d = sin L1 sin L2 + cos L1 cos L2 cos DLo: 1,855 M; 1,886 − 1,855 = 31 M saved.

q: You are planning the ARC crossing and want the great-circle distance from Las Palmas to Rodney Bay. What is it?

q: You plan the trade-wind crossing from Cocos (Keeling) to Mauritius. What is the great-circle distance?

q: You leave Falmouth westbound on the great circle for Newport, Rhode Island. What initial course do you steer?

o: Near Bermuda — the track runs south of east

q: You sail the great circle as rhumb-line legs between waypoints every 10° of longitude. How much farther is that than the true great circle?

o: Magnetic variation changes along the route

The Earth's rotation pulls the track to the right

q: Reaching the waypoint on 50°W, you check the great-circle course from here. What is it?

Two rhumb lines that meet at the vertex

q: You leave Las Palmas for St Lucia in late November. Why does your route head SSW for days instead of following the great circle?

o: To sail a shorter track than the great circle
To keep clear of the Canary Current
To pass the vertex of the great circle

q: You leave Honolulu for San Francisco in July. The NE trade blows straight down the great circle (054°T, 2,078 M) and the Pacific High lies across its middle. How do you route?

o: Along the great circle — the shortest is the fastest
South of the high, then north up the Californian coast
Along the rhumb line, then motor through the calms
why: Calms at the high's centre and a beat on the GC: sail north on the trade round the high, then east in the westerlies — more miles, fewer days.

South into the westerlies, then north up the Brazilian coast

The track is bent to keep inside the Aleutian ice limit

Yes — a steady course is always the shortest track
No — the rhumb line along 50°S is shorter still

C — where the line climbs back over 60°S

o: At X, the vertex, at about 43°45′S
Halfway across, where the line dips lowest
At Sydney — the track climbs north all the way

q: Bound from Salvador in Brazil to Grenada, you cross the equator. Which of the three tracks on this Mercator chart is the great circle?

o: B — the straight line between the two ports
C — bowed north of the straight line all the way

why: A GC bows towards the nearer pole: south of the rhumb line in the south, north of it past the equator — an S on the Mercator chart.

q: You plan the South Indian Ocean crossing from Durban to Fremantle. What is the great-circle distance?

It swings further south of east than 117°T
It comes round through 180° to west of south

You want one rhumb-line course from Honolulu to Suva by Mercator sailing, across the equator and the date line. What course and distance?
why: Contrary names add: DMP 2399.4, dLat 2,366′S; DLo 23°42′W = 1,422′; C = S 30.7° W; d = 2,366′ / cos C.

q: Your mate has worked the long rhumb line to Cape Town by plane sailing. You check it by Mercator sailing with the MPs. What do you find?
o: Same course and distance — both exact
why: Mercator: DMP 1463.7, DLo 4,575′ → 072°T, 3,498 M. Over a long leg the mean-latitude departure goes wrong.

q: You are about to cross the Bay of Biscay from Ushant to Cape Finisterre. Which sailing do you use to work the course and distance?
a: Plane sailing — on a leg this short it is close enough
o: Great circle sailing — nothing else is accurate
Composite sailing — to keep out of the bay
Parallel sailing — along the mean latitude
why: Plane sailing gives 208°T, 378 M and the GC is 378 M: over a few hundred miles the difference is a fraction of a mile.

q: East of Fiji you are on the parallel of Savusavu and will keep to it, across the 180° meridian, into the harbour. What distance is left?
why: DLo 2°30′ + 0°40′ = 3°10′ = 190′ across 180°; distance = DLo × cos lat = 190 × cos 16.78° = 182 M.

q: You plan to cross the Bay of Bengal westbound from Phuket to Galle in Sri Lanka. When do you go?
a: January — with the NE monsoon on the quarter
o: July — with the SW monsoon behind you
August — the SW monsoon is easing by then
Any month — the miles are the same
why: Westbound at 265°T the NE monsoon is on the quarter; in the SW monsoon the same great circle is a beat into F6–7 and rain.
ref: Great circle sailing — when it is not the best route

fig.title: Phuket → Galle, Sri Lanka
lines: NE monsoon Dec–Mar: fair, NE F3–5
SW monsoon Jun–Sep: W–SW F6–7, rain

q: In early June you are in Galle, bound for Salalah and the Red Sea. The great circle runs straight into the monsoon. What do you do?
a: Wait for the NE monsoon and go in January or February
o: Go now on the great circle — it is the shortest
Go now and motor close along the Indian coast
Go in August, when the monsoon has eased
why: In the SW monsoon the 295° track is a beat into F6–8 for 1,672 M; from December to March the NE monsoon puts the wind on the quarter.
ref: Great circle sailing — when it is not the best route

fig.title: Galle → Salalah, early June
lines: SW monsoon setting in: W–SW F6–8
July–August: the monsoon at its strongest

q: Leaving Fremantle for Mauritius in October, you compare the great circle with the trade-wind belt to the north. Which way do you route?
a: North-west into the SE trade, then west with it on the quarter
o: The great circle, due west along about 32°S
South into the westerlies, then north to Mauritius
North to the equator, then west along it
why: The GC runs through the light variables under the high; the SE trade to the north gives a fast reach — a few more miles, fewer days.
ref: Great circle sailing — when it is not the best route

fig.title: Fremantle → Mauritius, October
lines: Along 32°S: variable winds under the high

q: You plan Rio de Janeiro to Cape Town. The great circle runs east-south-east under the South Atlantic high, shown here. Which route do you take?
a: South of the high into the westerlies, then east to the Cape
o: The great circle — the shortest is the fastest
North of the high with the SE trade, then south
The rhumb line, motoring through the calms
why: Light winds lie under the high; to its south, near 35–40°S by Tristan da Cunha, the westerlies carry you east to the Cape.
ref: Great circle sailing — when it is not the best route

q: In May you leave New Zealand for Tahiti. The great circle heads north-east, straight into the SE trade. How do you route?
a: East in the westerlies to about 150°W, then north to Tahiti
o: The great circle — beat up it through the trade
North into the trade first, then east along 20°S
North to Tonga, then east along 18°S to Tahiti
why: Make your easting in the westerlies south of 30°S, then turn north and reach up through the SE trade: more miles, but no long beat.
ref: Great circle sailing — when it is not the best route
